claim: Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research's global creator population estimate is not an original measurement but is derived from its own prior estimate plus data from Zippia, a careers-content website, and Influencer Marketing Hub, a vendor survey publisher.
stance_target: The treatment of Goldman Sachs's 67 million / 107 million creator figures as independent institutional measurement
scope_conditions: Global; Goldman Sachs report 'Creator Economy: Framing Market Opportunity, Drivers of Content Creation/Distribution & Ads/Commerce', dated 26 March 2025, authored under Eric Sheridan's Americas Technology: Internet coverage
quoted_support: Leveraging our prior estimates (link) and data from Zippia (link), we estimate that there are ~67mm individuals who consider themselves "creators" globally in 2025 (up from ~50mm in 2022), which we expect to grow at an ~10% CAGR to reach ~107mm by 2030.
time_period: Published 26 March 2025; base year 2022; projection to 2030

claim: Goldman Sachs's own model projects that the absolute number of professional creators worldwide stays flat at 2.0 million from 2022 to 2025 while the total creator population grows from 50.0 million to 66.6 million, meaning every net entrant to content creation over that period was an amateur.
stance_target: The claim that growth in the creator population does not translate into growth in the number of people who make a living from it
scope_conditions: Global; Goldman Sachs exhibit with columns 2022 / 2025 / 2027 / 2030; 'Professional' and 'Amateur' assigned by respondent self-definition (full-time vs part-time), not by an income threshold; underlying data sourced to Zippia and Influencer Marketing Hub
quoted_support: Total Global Creators 50.0 / 66.6 / 80.5 / 107.2 ... Global "Professional" Creators 2.0 / 2.0 / 2.2 / 2.7 ... % of total 4.0% / 3.0% / 2.8% / 2.5%

claim: Goldman Sachs's professional/amateur split is defined by respondent self-identification as full-time or part-time, not by any income threshold, which contradicts Goldman's own 2023 public summary that described professionals as creators earning more than $100,000 a year.
stance_target: The widely-repeated claim that Goldman Sachs found ~4% of creators earn over $100,000 a year
scope_conditions: Global; footnote to the creator population exhibit in the 26 March 2025 Goldman Sachs report
quoted_support: "Professional" and "Amateur" based on self-deﬁnitions (e.g. full-time vs. part-time)

claim: The statistic that 3% of YouTubers capture 90% of net creator earnings, cited globally as Goldman Sachs research, is explicitly attributed inside the Goldman report to a Zippia study rather than to Goldman's own analysis.
stance_target: The attribution of the 3%/90% YouTube earnings concentration figure to Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research
scope_conditions: YouTube platform; Goldman Sachs report dated 26 March 2025; the underlying Zippia page is a 2023 statistics listicle, and the peer-reviewed study it derives from (Bärtl 2018) measured 85% of views, not 90% of earnings
quoted_support: to illustrate, according to the Zippia study above, 3% of YouTubers capture 90% of net creator earnings on the platform.
numbers: 85% of views in the underlying Bärtl 2018 study
time_period: Cited 2025; Zippia page 2023; underlying academic finding 2018

claim: Goldman Sachs identifies creator population growth as the direct mechanical cause of falling per-creator payouts, stating that the number of new creators joining platforms dilutes the payout of existing creators.
stance_target: The claim that creator income decline is a structural consequence of entry rather than individual failure
scope_conditions: Global; refers to fixed-pool creator funds including the closure of TikTok's and Meta's respective $1bn+ Creator Funds
quoted_support: we've seen a reduction in ﬁxed creator funds (with the closing of TikTok and Meta's respective $1bn+ Creator Funds), following increased pressure to compete for talent (with the number of new creators joining the platforms diluting the payout of existing creators).

claim: Goldman Sachs describes the creator earnings distribution as barbell-shaped, with a small percentage of creators capturing a significant percentage of overall earnings, and forecasts that amateur part-time creators will drive the majority of future population growth.
stance_target: The claim that creator income distributions are extremely right-skewed so that mean earnings are uninformative about typical outcomes
scope_conditions: Global; Goldman Sachs forecast horizon through 2030
quoted_support: a greater % of individuals consider themselves "amateur", or part-time creators vs. "professional", or full-time. This has driven a barbell-like distribution of creator earnings where a small % of creators capture a signiﬁcant % of overall earnings

claim: Private venture funding into creator-economy companies fell roughly 74% from its 2021 peak of approximately $3.6 billion to about $950 million in 2023 before partially recovering to roughly $1.5 billion in 2024.
stance_target: The claim that the creator economy has grown monotonically as an investable sector
scope_conditions: Content creation and creator platform companies; Goldman Sachs compilation; primarily US startup funding
quoted_support: Following a sizable increase in private market investment centered around the creator economy, funding slowed in 2022 and troughed in 2023. ... 2022 and ~$950mm in 2023, down from the peak of ~$3.6bn in 2021.

claim: Goldman Sachs cites eMarketer that total US influencer marketing spend was approximately $26 billion in 2023, about one-third of total US social digital ad spend, a US-specific figure that should not be extrapolated to other markets.
stance_target: The use of US influencer-marketing spend as a proxy for global creator earning opportunity
scope_conditions: United States only; 2023; eMarketer estimate cited within the Goldman report
quoted_support: eMarketer (link) estimates that total US inﬂuencer marketing was ~$26bn in 2023 or ~1/3 of total US social digital ad spend.
numbers: ~1/3 of US social digital ad spend

claim: Goldman Sachs's own exhibits show Patreon paid memberships rising steadily while monthly creator payouts remained relatively stable, indicating that per-creator and per-membership revenue on the leading direct-subscription platform is flat or declining as participation grows.
stance_target: The claim that platform growth does not raise typical creator earnings
scope_conditions: Patreon.com; Goldman Sachs Exhibits 9 and 10 in the March 2025 report; the exhibit series 13.4 to 15.6 (mm) tracks paid memberships, and the payouts series is presented separately in $mm; exact per-period mapping is not recoverable from extracted PDF text
quoted_support: Exhibit 9: Patreon.com Paid Memberships Have Increased Steadily... Exhibit 10: ...While Monthly Creator Payouts Have Remained Relatively Stable

claim: Goldman Sachs's operative definition of the creator economy is intent-based — individuals creating content with the goal of building an audience and monetizing their brand — which counts aspiration rather than realized earnings and therefore inflates the population relative to income-based definitions.
stance_target: The claim that creator population estimates diverge by an order of magnitude because of definitional choices rather than measurement error
scope_conditions: Global; definitional box in the March 2025 Goldman Sachs report
quoted_support: The creator economy is an ecosystem where individuals create content for digital consumption with the goal of building an audience base and monetizing their brand.
